text: Maintain a consistent sleep schedule: go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends.
Create a calming bedtime routine: dim lights, read or take a warm shower 30–60 minutes before bed; avoid screens.
Keep your bedroom cool (around 60–68°F / 15–20°C), dark, and quiet; consider blackout curtains, eye masks, and earplugs.
Avoid caffeine (coffee, black tea, some sodas) and nicotine at least 6–8 hours before bedtime.
Avoid heavy or spicy meals 2–3 hours before bedtime. If you're hungry, have a light carb+protein snack (e.g., yogurt with banana).
Limit alcohol near bedtime—while it can make you sleepy initially, it fragments sleep and reduces REM later in the night.
Aim for regular moderate exercise (30 minutes most days). Avoid intense workouts within 2-3 hours of bedtime.
If you have persistent daytime sleepiness, loud snoring, or witnessed breathing pauses, consult a sleep specialist for evaluation (possible sleep apnea).
Seek medical attention if you have new or severe insomnia that affects mood, work, or safety—consider referral to a clinician experienced in sleep disorders.
Practice relaxation techniques before bed: diaphragmatic breathing, guided imagery, progressive muscle relaxation, or short mindfulness meditation.
Limit naps to 20–30 minutes and earlier in the day; long or late naps can make it harder to fall asleep at night.
Include sleep-supportive nutrients: small amounts of tryptophan-rich foods (turkey, milk) and magnesium-rich foods (nuts, leafy greens).
Use a sleep diary or app to track bedtime, wake time, naps, caffeine, and alcohol—this helps identify patterns and triggers.
For evening meals, favor lighter proteins and complex carbs; avoid heavy sauces and fried foods close to bedtime.
If you have trouble sleeping, try morning or early afternoon exercise; gentle evening stretching can help relax muscles without overstimulation.
If stress or anxiety keeps you awake, create a 'worry journal' to offload concerns earlier in the evening and practice calming techniques.
Consider a primary-care consult if sleep problems persist—they can screen for medical causes (thyroid, depression, medications) and refer to specialists.
If you notice sudden weight gain, loud new snoring, or daytime breath-holding episodes, seek immediate medical evaluation for sleep apnea risk.
Limit screen exposure and blue light before bed; use night-shift display settings or blue-light filters if needed.
Avoid large amounts of liquids in the evening to reduce nighttime bathroom trips; hydrate earlier in the day.
Try cognitive-behavioral strategies for insomnia (CBT-I) if insomnia is chronic—it's effective and recommended before medication.
